analysis.one_liner: Rolls insulin list prices back to 2006 levels for manufacturers that certify, then bans rebates and insulin deductibles.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 54 cosponsors from both parties, but the two House committees it was sent to never acted on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Insulin list prices rose far above their 2006 levels while a system of behind-the-scenes rebates between drug makers and pharmacy benefit managers kept sticker prices high. This bill offered insulin manufacturers a deal: roll your list price back to what it was on July 1, 2006, and in return insurers and pharmacy benefit managers cannot take rebates on that insulin, cannot apply a deductible to it, and cannot kick it off formularies or impose new prior-authorization or step-therapy requirements for two years. The same rules would cover Medicare drug plans, and Medicaid rebates would be calculated from the manufacturer's pre-rollback price so states do not lose money. Manufacturers that certify could raise prices afterward only as fast as the medical care inflation index, and the HHS Inspector General could audit and fine those filing false data [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: People with diabetes who buy insulin. Certified insulin would carry a list price roughly what it was in 2006, the discount would be visible in the sticker price instead of hidden in rebates, and no deductible would apply to it, so patients would pay less at the counter from the first fill of the year [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with diabetes who use insulin

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers that roll the list price of an insulin back to its July 1, 2006 level become 'certified,' and insurers and pharmacy benefit managers are then barred from taking rebates or other remuneration on that insulin, except for discounts passed to the patient at the point of sale [S2] [S3].

Plans may not apply any deductible to certified insulin, with a conforming change so exempting insulin does not disqualify high-deductible health plans, meaning patients pay the certified price from their first purchase each year rather than paying full freight until a deductible is met [S3].

For the first two years an insulin is certified, plans cannot remove it from the formulary, raise its cost-sharing, or add new prior-authorization or step-therapy requirements, protecting patients from being switched off the affordable product [S3].

The same rebate ban and hold-harmless rules apply to Medicare prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans, and Medicaid's minimum rebate for certified insulin is computed from the manufacturer's pre-rollback price from late 2019, adjusted for inflation, so public programs do not lose value when list prices fall [S2] [S3].

To keep certification, a manufacturer may raise the list price no faster than the medical care component of the consumer price index, and the HHS Inspector General may audit manufacturers and fine those that submit false or incomplete price data [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers lose the rebate revenue they collect on insulin under the current list-price-and-rebate system. Insulin manufacturers that certify give up today's much higher list prices, though they gain a protected market position and a guaranteed annual price-increase allowance. Insurers would absorb some insulin cost earlier in the year because deductibles could not be applied to certified insulin [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and insulin makers

drawbacks.text: Participation is entirely voluntary: only manufacturers that certify a price rollback get the protections, and the bill contains no mechanism to force down the price of insulin from a manufacturer that declines to certify [S2] [S3].

Certified manufacturers may keep raising prices every year by the full increase in medical-care inflation, so the bill locks in annual increases rather than pushing prices back toward genuine production cost or toward competition from generics [S2] [S3].

The bill works entirely through the existing private insurance and pharmacy benefit manager structure, leaving those intermediaries in charge of formularies, cost-sharing, and administration rather than routing insulin through a direct public channel [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For insulin patients the upside is concrete and immediate: a sticker price near 2006 levels, no deductible, and two years of protection from being switched to a costlier product. The honest objection is that the deal is soft on manufacturers: it is voluntary, it lets them resume steady annual increases at the medical inflation rate, and it leaves the rebate-driven intermediary system intact for everything else. A patient paying hundreds of dollars a month for insulin would almost certainly be better off; the design gives away more long-term pricing power to participating manufacturers than a strictly competitive market would.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then to a Health subcommittee the next day, and neither panel ever held a markup or scheduled a vote before the two-year Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette, joined by Rep. Tom Reed, introduced the Insulin Price Reduction Act in the House on October 29, 2019 [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
The next day, October 30, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever taken on the bill [S5].

The bill finished with 54 cosponsors, 51 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a hearing in the record, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the insulin manufacturers kept the existing rebate system and high list prices, while people who buy insulin kept paying them. A bipartisan bill with 54 cosponsors never reached a vote in a Democratic-controlled House, so the intermediary rebate revenue and manufacturers' pricing latitude continued untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and insulin makers

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan, with 51 Democrats and 3 Republicans among the 54 cosponsors, but the bill died in committees chaired by Democrats without ever reaching a vote.

industries.note: PBM profits under the current system come from rebates negotiated off inflated insulin list prices; the bill bars PBMs from taking those rebates on certified insulin, allowing only transparent flat service fees and point-of-sale discounts. Patients pay the sticker price instead of financing hidden rebate revenue.

Manufacturers that certify give up today's inflated list prices, but in exchange get a formulary hold-harmless, an end to rebate extraction on their product, and a guaranteed annual price increase up to medical-CPI growth. Participation is voluntary, so a manufacturer can keep high prices simply by declining to certify.

Plans must forgo rebate remuneration on certified insulin and cannot apply deductibles to it, moving some insulin cost into the plan's base premium, but they also benefit from a permanently lower underlying drug price once prices reset.
